analysis.one_liner: Extends federal limits on steel imports for five more years.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 56 bipartisan Senate cosponsors but never received a committee vote and died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have extended the Steel Import Stabilization Act, the 1984 law that gives the President authority to limit how much foreign steel can enter the US market, for five additional years. Quotas on imported steel keep prices higher for American steelmakers and their workers, but everyone who buys steel — from car and appliance makers to homebuilders — pays more. The bill was introduced in February 1989 with 56 cosponsors from both parties and was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic steel producers and the workers in steel-producing regions: import limits shrink foreign competition, protecting US steelmakers' market share and the jobs that depend on it.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Steel Import Stabilization Act to extend that Act for a five-year period, stretching its authority from a fifth year through a tenth year.

The 1984 law it extends is the framework under which Presidents have limited steel imports to a negotiated share of the American market, so a five-year extension would have kept those limits in place through the mid-1990s.
Support was broad and bipartisan: the bill had 56 cosponsors, including 37 of the Senate's 55 Democrats and 19 of its 45 Republicans.

analysis.who_pays: Steel-using industries — construction, auto manufacturing, appliances, machinery — and ultimately consumers, who pay higher prices when import competition is capped. Foreign steel exporters also lose access to the US market.

drawbacks.text: Capping imports keeps steel prices above world levels, so the cost lands on American manufacturers that use steel and on consumers who buy cars, appliances, and homes built with pricier domestic steel.
Protection shields domestic producers from lower-cost foreign competition, which reduces the pressure on US steelmakers to cut costs and modernize.
The bill simply extended the existing law for five years without any new terms, locking in the arrangement rather than revisiting whether it was still working.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded higher steel prices for consumers and manufacturers against protected jobs in an industry hit hard by import competition in the 1980s. The gains were concentrated in steel-producing states and the costs were spread across everyone who buys steel products, which is the classic trade-off of import protection — defensible to its supporters, expensive to everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to the Finance Committee in February 1989, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. John Rockefeller introduced the bill on February 8, 1989, with 55 Senate cosponsors joining him.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee that same day.
The action history shows no further action — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — for the rest of the 101st Congress.
The underlying Steel Import Stabilization Act faced its own deadlines in this era, and Congress allowed this extension to lapse without ever bringing it to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Steel-importing manufacturers, foreign steel exporters, and consumers came out ahead, since import limits were never extended and steel prices stayed lower than a quota regime would have allowed. Steel producers and steel-region workers lost the extension they had lined up broad bipartisan support for.

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to extend the Steel Import Stabilization Act for five years.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lloyd Bentsen (D-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill never left committee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support split evenly across party lines — 37 of 55 Senate Democrats and 19 of 45 Senate Republicans cosponsored — and the bill's death was procedural, not a party vote.

industries.note: The bill would have extended for five more years the legal framework that caps foreign steel's share of the US market, keeping the industry's protected position and revenue in place. Its gain comes at consumers' expense through higher steel prices, though steelworker jobs ride on the same protection.
Import caps raise the price of their main input, so their costs and consumers' prices rise together. Killing the extension kept imported steel cheaper for them.
The extension would have kept quotas limiting their access to the US market for five more years; the bill's death preserved their ability to sell into the American market.
Import limits protect steel-producing jobs in regions like West Virginia and Pennsylvania. These workers gained from the bill and lost when it died.
